title: Experimental vs Observational Research

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Two ways to study whether a plant food helps tomatoes grow. First: walk the neighborhood, write down whose plants already got plant food, and measure heights. Second: hand out plant food yourself, so these ten pots get it and those ten do not. Only the second is an experiment, because you decided who got treated. When you make that decision, the two groups differ mainly in the one thing you handed out; when the world decides, they may differ in a dozen ways you never recorded.

### Question 2

A nature documentary crew can film wolves for years, use dozens of cameras, and track a huge pack, but they never tell a wolf what to eat. That is observation. Long follow-up and repeated measurement are just thoroughness; they do not turn watching into an experiment. The single question that settles the classification is whether the researcher decided who got the exposure. Here nobody handed out a menu, so it is observational no matter how many waves of data are collected.

### Question 3

Classifying an observational study is mostly a question of where the researcher started. Here they started at the ending: first collect the people who already have the infection, add a comparison set who do not, then work backward asking what each group was exposed to. Starting from the outcome is the signature of case-control. It is the practical choice when the outcome is rare, because waiting for 60 infections to appear in a followed group could take years.

### Question 4

Picking teams by letting friends group up produces one stacked side. Flipping a coin for each player instead sprinkles the tall, fast, and slow players across both sides without anyone planning it. Random assignment does the same for study participants, including traits nobody thought to measure. Note what it does not do: it splits the people you already enrolled, so it cannot make an unrepresentative sample representative, and it cannot stop people from dropping out later.

### Question 5

Both teams are solving the same puzzle from opposite ends. The cohort team starts with who was exposed and waits to see who develops the outcome, which lets them watch new cases accumulate over the 5 years. The case-control team starts with who already has the outcome and reconstructs exposures, which is faster but relies on records or recall. Neither team ever assigned the exposure, so the choice between them is about direction and efficiency, not about experimenting.

### Question 6

There are two things a researcher can control: whether an intervention is delivered, and how people land in the groups. A true experiment controls both. Pure observation controls neither. This study sits in between, because the researcher handed out the training but let the staffing rosters decide who received it. That middle category has its own name, quasi-experimental, and its weakness is specific: whatever already made Clinic A different from Clinic B travels with the results.

### Question 7

Water one houseplant with a new fertilizer and it grows two inches in a month. Impressive, until you remember plants grow anyway. The 60 untreated participants are the second plant: they show how much change happens from time passing, from getting measured twice, and from ordinary improvement. Subtract their change from the treated group's change and what remains is attributable to the intervention. With one group there is nothing to subtract.

### Question 8

Three of these studies compare people who already walk with people who already do not, which means they are also comparing whatever else makes someone a walker. The fourth hands out the assignment by chance: you walk, you stretch, you carry on as usual. Ask one question of any study description, who decided which condition each person was in. If the answer is the researcher, it is experimental; if the answer is the participant or their circumstances, it is observational.

### Question 9

You would never test whether a solvent causes cancer by asking volunteers to breathe it for 40 years, so the trial that would give the cleanest answer is the one you are not allowed to run. What remains is to study people whose jobs already exposed them and compare their outcomes with similar unexposed workers. The trade-off is honest: nobody was put at risk by the study, but because the researcher did not control exposure, other differences between exposed and unexposed workers must be accounted for.

### Question 10

A class photo shows who is tall and who wears glasses on one day, but it cannot show who grew first. Measuring weight and back pain in 300 patients in one afternoon is the same kind of snapshot: it tells you how common back pain is right now, not whether body mass index came before the pain. The single time point is what makes it cross-sectional, and the absence of any assignment is what makes it observational.

### Question 11

A wind tunnel test of a paper airplane changes one thing at a time, so you know exactly what caused what, but you can only test a few planes under artificial air. A school-wide field day gives thousands of flights in real wind, but throwers, paper, and gusts all vary at once. Fifty times more flights does not tell you which factor mattered. Scale buys precision and realism; assignment buys the ability to say the intervention caused the difference.

### Question 12

At present the clinics are choosing the new method themselves, and clinics eager to adopt something new probably differ from cautious ones in staffing, leadership, and patient mix. Watching longer, watching more sites, or adjusting for age afterward cannot undo who chose what, because adjustment only fixes differences you thought to measure. Drawing 3 clinic names for the new method replaces self-selection with chance, and that single move is what makes the design experimental.
